decisions.quote: The primary purpose of this study was the use of a number-line assessment to replicate the logarithmic-to-linear shift pattern in positive number sense explored by Booth and Siegler (2006), as well as to examine the hypothesized parallel logarithmic-to-linear shift using negative numbers.
decisions.reason: The shipped row misidentified Siegler & Opfer (2003) as the replicated original because it was the only citation appearing in the abstract's background sentence ('Numerical estimation has been used to study how children mentally represent numbers for many years (e.g., Siegler & Opfer, 2003)'). In the full text, Siegler & Opfer (2003) is cited only as general background on numerical estimation tasks, whereas the authors explicitly identify Booth & Siegler (2006) as the primary study whose logarithmic-to-linear shift pattern in positive number sense they set out to replicate (Introduction, p. 343), follow its analytic model and test whether its age-related shift could be replicated (Results, p. 346), and state their overall positive-number replication verdict specifically citing Booth & Siegler (2006) (Discussion, p. 354). While the Method section (p. 344) also notes adopting the 0–1,000 task values from Opfer & Siegler (2007) (blind target_index 1), only row 2447 is requested and Booth & Siegler (2006) (blind target_index 0) is the primary tested original replacing the shipped abstract-level misattribution.

decisions.quote: Our findings replicate those of Siegler and colleagues (e.g., Booth & Siegler, 2006) for positive numbers; specifically, we found evidence of a shift from logarithmic to linear representations for positive numbers between fourth and sixth grade (0–1,000 scale). More interestingly, we found a similar pattern of results for negative numbers. While the second graders’estimations were best fit by a logarithmic function for negative number lines, the fourth and sixth graders’estimations were best fit by a linear function.
decisions.reason: After resolving the tested original for row 2447 to Booth & Siegler (2006) (and noting that the same verdict holds for Opfer & Siegler, 2007), the authors state an explicit overall replication verdict in both the Abstract and the Discussion that their results replicated the shift from logarithmic to linear representations for positive numbers on the 0–1,000 scale, supported by the increase in estimation accuracy across grades and the shift from logarithmic best fit in Grade 2 to linear best fit in Grades 4 and 6.

decisions.quote: The present study tested children in the 2nd, 4th, and 6th grades to assess their mental representations of both positive and negative numbers using a standard numerical estimation task. We replicated the shift from a logarithmic to linear representation for positive numbers (0–1,000 scale) in that 2nd graders represented positive numbers logarithmically, but 4th and 6th graders represented the numbers linearly.
decisions.reason: The authors collected new empirical data from 241 elementary and middle school students (Grades 2, 4, and 6) on a number-line estimation task to re-test the previously published logarithmic-to-linear developmental shift in positive number estimation (Booth & Siegler, 2006; Opfer & Siegler, 2007) and extend it to negative numbers, making this a replication.

corrected_value.authors: Opfer, J. E., & Siegler, R. S.
corrected_value.title: Representational change and children’s numerical estimation.

decisions.quote: We used the same values as Opfer and Siegler, which allowed for better discrimination between logarithmic and linear representations. Positive values included 2, 5, 18, 34, 56, 78, 100, 122, 147,150, 163, 179, 246, 366, 486, 606, 722, 725, 738, 754, 818, and 938. Negative values were exactly the same but were presented with a negative sign. Given the variety of number estimation tasks that exist and the importance of the type of task for this skill (see Cohen & Sarnecka, 2014), we chose to use two separate lines (positive and negative) for two reasons. First, we wanted to directly replicate Siegler’s work (Opfer & Siegler, 2007)as closely as possible and thus chose to use the original positive number line and values used in those studies.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. In the Method (p. 344) and Discussion (pp. 354–355), the authors explicitly state that they designed the positive 0–1,000 number-line task and 22 target values to directly replicate Opfer and Siegler (2007) as closely as possible and to provide a direct comparison to those findings, testing logarithmic versus linear estimation fits in 2nd, 4th, and 6th graders. The reference list (p. 357) establishes the original identity as Opfer, J. E., & Siegler, R. S. (2007), 'Representational change and children’s numerical estimation,' Cognitive Psychology, 55, 169–195 (no DOI printed in source). This 2007 Cognitive Psychology study is a separate independent work from shipped row 2447 (Siegler & Opfer, 2003, Psychological Science, 14, 237–243, 10.1111/1467-9280.02438) and from sibling target 0 (Booth & Siegler, 2006, Developmental Psychology, 41, 189–201), all three of which appear as distinct entries in the paper's reference list; report equivalence does not apply.

initial_expert_decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. In the Introduction (p. 343), Results (p. 346), and Discussion (p. 354), Brez, Miller, and Ramirez (2016) explicitly re-test Booth and Siegler's (2006) empirical findings on the 0–1,000 positive number-line estimation task in a new sample of 2nd, 4th, and 6th graders (N = 241), comparing grade-level reductions in percent absolute error and paired-sample t-test comparisons of logarithmic versus linear model fits across grades. The reference list (p. 357) establishes the original identity as Booth, J. L., & Siegler, R. S. (2006), 'Developmental and individual differences in pure numerical estimation,' Developmental Psychology, 41, 189–201 (no DOI printed in source). The sole shipped row 2447 is Siegler & Opfer (2003, 'The Development of Numerical Estimation', Psychological Science, 14, 237–243, 10.1111/1467-9280.02438), which is a separate earlier paper also cited independently in the reference list, and sibling target 1 (Opfer & Siegler, 2007, Cognitive Psychology, 55, 169–195) is a distinct third publication; thus report equivalence does not apply and Booth & Siegler (2006) is a genuinely absent original.
